chapters.title: Aim higher. Then sound like you mean it.
chapters.intro: Once the first sales are real, I want the next target to stretch me. And when I explain an offer, I want the buyer to hear somebody who knows what they are doing.
chapters.takeaway: Aim beyond the first success, but let a clear offer and real ability carry the confidence.
chapters.body:
If I am doing a good job, selling a good product, and reaching people across the world, why would I think only about a tiny result? A bigger market gives me room to think bigger. But there is a difference between aiming high and talking b*llshit. If I have sold nothing, I should not walk around discussing half-a-million turnover as though it is already sitting in the bank.

The order matters. Get something working. Then push it further. Suppose I get to $1,000 a day, or $2,000 a day. I can enjoy that progress without deciding the business is finished. Where can I improve the offer? Where is the next customer? What part of the system is holding the rest back? Aim higher all of the time.

I want that ambition to show in how I speak. Think about going to a surgeon. Do I want someone stumbling through an explanation, sounding frightened of their own job? Or someone who can calmly explain what will happen and why they can handle it? When a buyer is about to hand over money, confidence can remove a lot of doubt.

People love confidence.

When I was selling television advertising, I went into meetings and said we were the best at our price and at the way we planned the media. I was relatively new. I did not have an independent table proving I was the best in the country. I said it with conviction, and the buyer did not have my knowledge of the industry to challenge every detail.

That story shows how powerful delivery can be. It also shows the difference between a strong presentation and proof. Calling myself the best does not make the comparison true. If I am asking for trust, the actual offer still has to survive the questions after the confident opening.

So you have to be confident in your delivery.

I do not need to fill every sentence with um, maybe, I think, perhaps. I can say what I do, what it costs, and why it suits the buyer. I can answer the question directly, then stop talking. Calm does more for me than a long apology for being in the room.

So I want ambition without fantasy, and confidence without empty noise. If I can do the job, I should sound like I can do the job. If there is a limit, I should know what it is. A smooth voice helps me open the door; the work is what keeps it open.

figures.caption: The delivery can be strong while the claim still needs support.

items.label: Clear confidence
items.text: I know the work, explain the value, and answer the question directly.

items.label: Empty superiority
items.text: I announce I am the best, but offer nothing the buyer can check.

chapters.title: Follow the money. Share the knowledge.
chapters.intro: I do not receive money because I have a company name. Someone has to decide that what I provide is worth paying for. And the method cannot live inside one person forever.
chapters.takeaway: Know why the buyer pays, and make the working method available beyond one key person.
chapters.body:
I remember being twenty, looking at the television agency, the cars, the office, and the money moving through the account. We did not have proper profit, but there was money everywhere. I asked my business partner how the h*ll that had happened.

He gave me a simple picture. Money is like water. Water leaves the sea, becomes a cloud, falls as rain, runs through a river, reaches a pond, and moves again. If I stand in the right place, at the right time, I get wet. That was his way of explaining trade: find where money is already moving and put something useful in its path.

Why are they going to give you their money?

I cannot just announce that I am making money and expect it to appear. An actual person has to part with it. A buyer has a problem or a desire. A supplier has something that could help. Sometimes I am useful because I connect the two. I do not have to own the factory to create a worthwhile transaction.

So I put the business into plain words: I have this. I am selling it to this person. They will pay me because of these reasons. If I cannot finish that sentence, I have found a hole in the business. A logo does not fill that hole. Neither does an office.

Now look inside the company. I have seen people become so busy that an assistant knows every password and the owner knows none of them. The assistant is excellent, so nobody notices the problem. Then the assistant leaves. Suddenly being busy looks a lot like having given away control.

Don't make anyone irreplaceable.

We had a salesman who was better than the others. When he left, we really suffered. What I should have done was ask him to teach the team. Every Friday morning, explain the pitch. Show them what you say when someone objects. Tell them where you pause. Let the others hear the part that works.

I could have offered Friday afternoon off, extra money, lunch, or another benefit for that work. I could have made passing on the method part of his role. Instead, too much of the company's ability walked out with one person.

I want good people. Of course I do. But I also want a business that can carry on when someone is sick, away, or ready to move on. Respect the person, reward the skill, and let the knowledge spread. A strong team should not be one good worker surrounded by people who have never been shown how the job works.

chapters.title: Wanting it is one thing. Doing it is another.
chapters.intro: A real limit can sharpen a buying decision. But all the urgency in the world means nothing if I keep talking about a business and never take the first step.
chapters.takeaway: Make genuine availability clear, then stop confusing an idea with an action.
chapters.body:
Imagine someone calls asking for two pieces of equipment. I say I need to check availability because demand has been high. Before I disappear to check, I ask what they need the equipment for. Now the customer is explaining the reason for the purchase in their own words.

There are two things happening. They are remembering the need, and they are considering what happens if the item is unavailable. Later, if I call back and say I can get two, the next question is whether they are ready to purchase. That question moves the conversation from vague interest to a decision.

You already have the idea.

I have used the take-away idea in sales: people can want something more when they think they may not get it. But if I pretend stock is missing when it is not, I am making up the reason to hurry. The useful part is understanding the buyer's need and communicating a real limit clearly.

A $17 electronic book makes the point. It is a file. Saying it will somehow run out forever sounds ridiculous. A genuine cap on something scarce is a different matter. The reason for the limit has to make sense. Otherwise the buyer can see the trick before I have even reached the payment page.

Now turn the pressure back towards me. I can spend all day thinking about how to persuade a customer while doing absolutely nothing to create the offer. I had a conversation with a woman who wanted a cosmetics business. She said she did not know what to do. So I gave her a simple starting route.

Get samples from a supplier. Find something she likes. Decide on the presentation. Make the website. Speak to creators who already discuss cosmetics. Find out whether people want the product. A week later I asked how much she had sold.

“What do you mean?”

Seven days had passed and she had done nothing. Not a sample. Not a page. Not a conversation with a buyer. The missing ingredient was not another clever explanation. It was the first piece of work.

That outline is a starting test, not an entire finished cosmetics operation. The product still has to be suitable, the claims true, and delivery possible. But even those questions can be worked on. Sitting still does not answer them.

I put my own idea into motion within roughly thirty-two to thirty-four hours: an advert, a website, enrolment, and filming. The exact rush is less important than the contrast. I had started building the thing while other people would still have been describing what they might build.

Too much waiting, too much talking, not enough action.

I am not asking for a perfect company by tonight. I am asking for something I can point at. A sample ordered. A useful conversation finished. A page that explains the offer. A real attempt gives me information. Another week of talking gives me another week of talking.

chapters.title: Sell something people want. Know what the attention is for.
chapters.intro: I do not need a glamorous product. I need demand, a way to reach it, and a reason for the buyer to trust the offer. Attention is only useful when I know where I want it to go.
chapters.takeaway: Connect the product, the audience, and the commercial objective before chasing attention.
chapters.body:
Why am I running a business? For me, the answer is money. I do not need to fall in love with every object I sell. Someone can make a fortune selling concrete without wanting to hug a block of concrete at night. An ordinary product can sit inside a very good business.

I use cosmetics as another example because I do not wear them. I would need people who understand the product, but the commercial questions would still be familiar. Where are the buyers? What do they want? How do I get the first orders? Can I deliver the offer at a worthwhile margin?

It doesn't matter what you sell. It matters that it sells.

Liking a subject is useful. It is not proof that customers want my version of it. And knowing how to sell does not remove the need to understand what I have promised. I want the enthusiasm pointed towards a working business, rather than towards owning a product I happen to like.

Now suppose I am using social media. People get pulled into public arguments because the argument itself feels like activity. They keep answering, keep jabbing, keep checking the replies. At the end, what did they want to achieve? More attention? More sales? A change in how people see them? If they cannot answer, they have no end point.

When I used conflict for attention, I had a commercial objective. In one argument with a science-fiction fan community, I wanted the attention to lead towards a relationship course. I think that weekend brought in around 15,000 in sales. I had an audience, an offer, and a reason to connect the two. An argument without that connection is just an argument.

Have a clear end goal. Have a clear objective.

I also had my own rough audience rule: I did not want to spend time fighting with an account below 10,000 followers. That was how I weighed the reach. But follower count alone cannot tell me whether the argument is worthwhile. A big audience that hates the offer can still be the wrong audience, and a fight can damage trust faster than it brings business.

There is a quieter way to create interest: show that other people already buy. With television advertising I would mention other campaigns and the clients we were working with. I might describe fifteen sign-ups in two weeks, or explain why a period was busy. A buyer could see that the company was real and that other people had made a similar decision.

I used seasonal conversations too. If someone said it was only March, I would talk about businesses already preparing their Christmas campaigns. Even in January, I could turn the conversation towards the next seasonal push. The pressure came from the thought that competitors were already moving. But that story has to be true; a confident seasonal line is not evidence that the whole market is ahead.

I put purchase notifications on my site for the same reason: visible activity makes the offer feel less lonely. I do not have to say a digital door closes at midnight if genuine customer activity already shows interest. Real proof reduces uncertainty. An invented countdown just adds noise.

chapters.title: When the old route breaks, find the new need.
chapters.intro: A problem can close one route and make another need obvious. I look at what people still have, what they have lost, and what useful connection I can make.
chapters.takeaway: Look for the need created by a change, then build a clear offer around it.
chapters.body:
Things go wrong inside businesses. Things also go wrong across whole markets. I can sit there being angry about the mess, or I can ask what the mess has made people need. First fix the immediate problem. Then look at whether the response could also improve the business.

Take a shop with a weak back-end system and missing customer information. I used a rough example of a face product normally priced at 10.99, offered at 0.99 when someone buys another item. Even if that promotion only breaks even, it can create fresh orders and bring existing customers back into the habit of buying.

Chaos in the industry is an opportunity.

It does not magically recover old records. A new order is a new order. What it can do is restart a customer conversation and create current information through an actual purchase. The useful point is that a repair or reactivation effort may have more value than its immediate profit line.

Now make the problem bigger. Imagine travel is disrupted and people spend days stuck at airports. The next time they buy a ticket, the memory is still there. What was once a distant risk now feels real. I would look at a partnership with an insurer that can provide properly defined disruption cover. The airline has customers with a newly obvious concern; the specialist has a way to cover it.

I am thinking on my feet in that example. I have not proved that a particular policy exists or that every event would be covered. The business idea is the connection: a painful experience changes what customers value, and a suitable partner can help meet that need.

My next example is creators losing advertising income. They still have viewers. They still have people who like their work. What has disappeared is one way of turning those viewers into money. Merchandise becomes interesting because it uses something they still have: an audience.

Suppose I know ten other large creators. I speak to a merchandise supplier about my own products, then ask about introducing the others. If those introductions are valuable, I can discuss a share of the turnover I bring in. In my example, I asked for five percent.

Before that conversation, I just knew the other creators. After a clear agreement, I could be providing a route they needed, a customer group the supplier wanted, and an income stream tied to the connection. I have not invented a new audience. I have helped an existing audience support a different offer.

That is what I mean by looking for opportunity in chaos. I do not need to pretend the disruption is good. I need to notice what has changed. What do people still have? What are they suddenly missing? Who can genuinely supply it? Those questions can be more useful than repeating that the market used to be easier.

chapters.title: The detail I love may mean nothing to the buyer.
chapters.intro: I can know everything about my product and still explain it badly. If the buyer cannot see why a difference matters, I have not given them a reason to pay for it.
chapters.takeaway: Translate the useful difference into something the buyer can understand and care about.
chapters.body:
There is a simple picture behind every sale. The customer has money. I have an offer. The customer decides whether to exchange one for the other. That decision happens inside their head, with their knowledge, their priorities, and their doubts. It does not happen inside mine.

Take a massage business. I might be proud of using an expensive oil. I have read about it, compared it with other oils, and decided it is better. So I put it at the centre of the business and charge more. Then a customer looks at me and the cheaper place down the road. To them, oil is oil.

“But ours is the best.”
“Fine. What difference will I notice?”

That is where the explanation usually falls apart. I am answering as the person who bought the oil, rather than the person buying the massage. The customer may never have tried a bad oil. They may not know what the terms on the bottle mean. They may not even know why different kinds of massage have different names.

Always look from your buyer's eyes.

I have two basic choices. Explain a real difference that matters to them, in words they understand, or stop treating an invisible feature as the reason they should pay more. I do not get to charge for my private excitement and then blame the customer for failing to share it.

Suppose the competing service is $20 cheaper. If the only difference the buyer can identify is the price, why would they choose mine? I have said before that I do not want price to be my only selling point. Then I have work to do: make the other reason visible.

I can make bold-sounding claims about skin and results, but a good sentence is not a guarantee. I need a benefit I can actually support. Otherwise I have turned the problem of unclear value into a different problem: promising something I cannot establish.

Now walk past a coffee shop. What makes me step inside? The chairs look comfortable. The room looks warm. The lights make it inviting. The cups have some character. The welcome seems pleasant. The decision can be shaped by small visible things before I have tasted the coffee.

I need that same level of care with my own offer. What does the buyer see first? What do they understand? Why would they choose me rather than somebody else? The detail can be excellent and still need an explanation. My knowledge is useful only when I turn it into a reason the customer can recognise.

chapters.title: Ask someone who does not speak my business language.
chapters.intro: I run ideas past my mother because she will ask the simple question I have made complicated. An honest outsider can show me what my explanation is missing.
chapters.takeaway: Listen for the reason someone would actually buy, and the reason they would walk away.
chapters.body:
I have gone to my mother with business ideas because she does not automatically think like an insider. She is not impressed by the same technical detail I am impressed by. She wants to know what it does, what it costs, and why anybody would want it. That can be very useful.

Imagine I tell her I am opening a massage business. She asks the price. Then she says it sounds expensive. I jump in with my proud explanation of the best massage oil. She asks what is different about the oil. In a few seconds, she has found two things I need to explain: why the price makes sense, and why that ingredient should matter.

Start writing down all the reasons she wouldn't buy from you.

I can call that question basic. It is basic. That is the point. The customer may ask exactly the same thing. I have had plenty of massages while training as a fighter, and even I can walk in, hear a list of different treatments, and still not know which one I need. Experience of buying something does not always produce specialist knowledge.

I do not stop at “What do you think?” People can be polite. They can like me, like the idea, and still never buy. I ask the next question.

well, would you buy from me?

If the answer is no, I want the reason. No time? The visit is inconvenient? The booking looks awkward? The difference is unclear? Those are more useful answers than a warm compliment about how enterprising I am.

In the massage conversation, no time to travel could lead to a mobile service. Difficulty booking could lead to a clear flyer and booking by text message. I am not arguing with the objection. I am learning where the offer creates work for the buyer, then seeing whether I can remove that work.

I remember taking a new sports car to my mother's house. She asked how much it had cost. I told her 300,000. She came outside, looked at it, and asked why I had paid so much for something with only two seats. By her way of measuring it, more money should have bought more useful places to sit. I could have bought a bus.

I cared about one set of qualities. She saw a completely different set. It was funny, but it was also a reminder. A customer does not have to use my private scorecard.

A family member cannot stand in for every specialist customer. But if I cannot explain an ordinary offer to a candid person outside the business, that tells me something. Write down the words they use. The reasons they would buy can become clearer selling points. The reasons they would not buy can become the next problems to solve.

chapters.title: The little office, the pizza, and the ten-day absence.
chapters.short: Community and the leader who vanished
chapters.intro: After my first agency, I tried a different sales setup. The team stayed close to the energy in the room. When we left, I found out how much of the business depended on us being there.
chapters.takeaway: Pay matters, and so do direction, belonging, recognition, and continuity.
chapters.body:
After the first television business, I found an office in Luton for £400 a month. My brother and I sat there and advertised for commission-only sales staff. I wanted to build another advertising company, but I changed the way the work was divided.

In the earlier business, everyone had to pitch on the phone. We spent two hours a day training people to do it. Cold calling is hard to teach. Some people are frightened of it. Some can speak well but struggle with the particular pitch. So the new idea was to separate finding an interested contact from handling the call.

The team looked for marketing managers and sent emails. If a manager replied, I took the phone conversation. I was already trained at that part. Instead of asking every beginner to become a complete salesperson immediately, I had them find an opening that I could work on.

Money is numbers. And numbers never end.

We looked through magazines and websites for suitable businesses. One useful clue was a store locator. A company with several branches might have more use for national television advertising than a single little shop. We still had to find the current person responsible for marketing. Bought contact lists could be out of date because people changed jobs.

The commission was five percent. A £20,000 deal meant £1,000 for the person who brought it in. Two of those in a month meant £2,000. But a possible commission was not the same as money already earned.

People joined and people left. Eventually there were four men with us, six people in the office altogether. They were working through the contacts, and for the first solid month most of them did not make anything. I kept the atmosphere moving. I came in full of energy, talked about the replies, and told them where I thought the next deal would come from.

I ordered pizza. We sat around eating it while I talked about the company we were building. I compared the old business with what this one could become. For about a ten-dollar pizza each day, I had a shared moment that made a bare office feel more like a team.

Then I accepted a fight and went away to train in Slovakia. My brother came too. We were away for ten days. Every one of those men left. The business fell apart.

The leaders had abandoned ship.

There was no daily energy, no clear next conversation, and no one creating that sense that the work was going somewhere. The obvious question finally filled the room: why am I here doing this without pay? I had built something that depended far too heavily on our presence and on a future promise.

So when I talk about motivation beyond money, I am not saying a pizza replaces wages. Obviously, pay your staff well. I am saying more money alone will not fix a job where people hate the work, hate the treatment, and cannot see a direction.

I saw a similar mistake with people launching a fight promotion. They thought paying the biggest purse would automatically bring the best fighters. But the event lacked exposure, production, and prestige. Some fighters preferred a better-known stage because of what winning there could do for their career. People can value the money and still care about the place the work takes them.

chapters.title: The next attempt gets faster. The offer still has to matter.
chapters.intro: The first time, I am building the method as well as doing the work. Repetition makes me faster. But all that skill still has to lead to an offer somebody values enough to choose.
chapters.takeaway: Reuse what I learn, and distinguish a priority objection from a genuine lack of budget.
chapters.body:
Success is exponential.

That is how I describe the feeling of doing something I have already learned. The first parallel park takes ages. Later it becomes ordinary. The first website means finding people, discovering what is missing, making mistakes, and fixing them. By the third, fourth, or fifth site, I know who to call and which problems to prevent.

The first business has to create contacts and methods that do not exist yet. Later, I can use them again. I can give the right tasks to people I already know. I could get a small new setup moving in about six hours because the people and the working relationships were already there.

The problems change.

That is the useful part of the word exponential here. I am describing accumulated experience, not giving you a mathematical promise that every month doubles. The problems can change as the business grows. Delivery, money, and the amount of coordination all change. It can still become easier to repeat a particular job because I am no longer solving it from scratch.

Now think about the person on the other side. I hear “I cannot afford it,” and I want to understand what that means. Sometimes there is simply no available money. Sometimes there is money, but the buyer has decided that something else matters more. Those are different situations.

I have used the comparison with nights out or expensive meals. If someone values a course more, they may choose it instead of those things. I am asking them to make a trade between priorities. But paying rent or buying food is not the same kind of optional choice. I cannot prove someone has a spare budget just because they are still meeting basic needs.

Consider the industrial pipe example. A buyer says the new pipe costs too much. If the replacement genuinely lowers operating costs, then the cost of keeping the old one belongs in the conversation. The question becomes whether the savings are real and whether the buyer can fund the change, rather than whether the invoice looks large on its own.

I knew someone selling gas and oil supplies, so that was the kind of offer I had in mind. I was not reporting his actual sales script. I was showing how an objection about money can also be a question about value over time.

I also ran an adult-entertainment business during a recession and still saw customers spend. That taught me not to assume every market had stopped just because the wider economy was difficult. It did not tell me every person was comfortable, or that any business could ignore a downturn. My customers were a particular group making a particular choice.

I want to know which problem I am facing. Is the offer unclear? Is the customer the wrong fit? Is another purchase more urgent? Or is the budget really unavailable? If I answer all of those with the same pushy line, I have stopped listening. Better selling starts with understanding the decision I am actually asking someone to make.

chapters.title: Nothing fixes itself while I make excuses.
chapters.intro: A broken process needs someone to own the next step. I would rather try a small change quickly than watch a quiet period become a quiet month.
chapters.takeaway: Take responsibility for the repair, keep the experiment affordable, and pay attention to what actually changed.
chapters.body:
When did I last get a flat tyre, leave the car alone, and come back to find the tyre had repaired itself? It does not work like that. Yet people treat business problems as though enough waiting will turn them into solutions.

Someone tells me sales have been slow for a couple of months. I ask what they have done about it. They say they are thinking of placing some adverts. Months have already passed. I would have been asking questions after the second slow day.

That does not mean I know every quiet day is a disaster. It means I do not want to use normal variation as a reason never to inspect anything. Is the purchase route working? Are enquiries being answered? Has the presentation become stale? What can I check today?

Nothing ever fixes itself.

The same goes for technical trouble. A payment service is stuck, or hosting is not working, and I am told somebody is looking at it. Fine. Who owns the next action? When will I hear back? I have waited for other people enough times to know that a vague promise can stay vague for a very long time. Persistent follow-up keeps the problem visible.

My brother and I used to disagree about quiet days in the studio business. After three or four of them, I wanted to change things. He might say there had been a big football match and customers were busy. I would look at an account score, a set that had looked the same for a year, a costume, or the way a performer was presenting herself.

We changed wallpaper, adjusted the furniture, changed an account, and tried a different look. A ten-dollar costume. About twenty dollars spent altogether. Later, the money improved.

“Maybe it was the changes. Maybe the quiet period would have ended anyway.”

That was my brother's point, and it is a real question. I changed several things at once. The improvement happened after those changes, but that alone cannot tell me which one mattered, or whether another event had changed demand.

I was proud that I had acted instead of sitting there. I still want that bias towards a useful, affordable move. But I do not get a clearer answer by declaring that everything was definitely down to me. The next time, I want to remember what I changed and what happened around it.

My argument was never that panic should send me out to blow a fortune on advertising. I was asking what I could do with the things already in front of me. Find a problem, take a small step, and learn. Waiting has a cost. Random expensive movement has a cost too. I want the repair to improve the business, rather than just make me feel busy.

chapters.title: Make it easy for the right customer to pay.
chapters.intro: I can lose a deal because I am rigid about the route, even when the customer has something of real value. My job is to understand the exchange, the cost, and whether I can actually deliver.
chapters.takeaway: Remove unnecessary payment friction, and count what turns into usable money.
chapters.body:
I had a business card that made people ask whether I was joking. It listed all sorts of impossible-sounding tasks. The point was not that I personally knew every trade in the world. The point was that I wanted to be the person who would work out a route if the task and the price made sense.

I dictate my prices.

Suppose somebody wanted a difficult offshore project built. I used an absurdly large invoice, $6.6 billion, to make the example memorable. Or suppose they wanted a rocket sent to the moon. If I received six billion and a capable specialist could do the work for five billion, the connection would be the business.

Those were exaggerated illustrations, not projects I had actually completed. The everyday point is smaller. I do not have to say no immediately because I cannot personally perform every part. I can look at a suitable specialist, the real delivery cost, and what I am being asked to take responsibility for. A big invoice does not make an impossible promise possible by itself.

Then there is the simpler way people say no: they make paying awkward. The customer wants a direct transfer, but the site only accepts one route. The buyer has another currency, but nobody can explain the conversion. The purchase is ready, yet the path to completing it is a wall.

It has to be very, very easy to give you money.

I want a bridge. I have met people in person to accept payment. I have considered different currencies and other forms of value. I even used two truckloads of laundry detergent worth $5,000 as an example. If somebody has valuable stock rather than cash, the question is whether that value can actually be used or sold, rather than whether it looks like the usual payment screen.

My friend running fight shows gave me the clearest story. A sponsor wanted its name on the cage and on television. But instead of paying cash, the sponsor wanted to supply roof tiles. My friend could refuse and lose the sponsor, or work out whether the tiles were useful to somebody else.

So he accepted the stock and made calls. In the example, the tiles had a stated value of $5,000. He could offer them for $4,500 to someone who would collect them. He gave up $500 of that stated value, but turned the arrangement into cash and kept the sponsor.

That is a real distinction. Five thousand printed on a stock valuation is not the same as five thousand spendable in the account. Moving, storing, valuing, and selling the goods can cost effort too. I need to count the amount I can actually recover.

Be easy to do business with. That is the part worth keeping. I do not make a good deal better by ignoring the conditions around payment or delivery. I make it better by finding a workable route and understanding what that route really costs.

chapters.title: One closed door should not close the whole business.
chapters.intro: If every customer, payment, and audience connection depends on one service, one failure can stop everything. I want alternatives ready before I need them.
chapters.takeaway: Map the dependencies and build legitimate alternatives for the ones that could stop the business.
chapters.body:
The roof-tile story leads to another point. My friend did not have only one way to create value from a show. He could work with sponsors in different forms. In my exaggerated picture, he could end up with four hundred bottles of alcohol, timber, and enough roof tiles for three medium-sized homes. That was my way of saying the business had more than one route through the world.

I want that same thinking around money and attention. If one payment service stops working, what happens? If a bank arrangement is interrupted, what work can continue? If a social account disappears, can the audience still find me anywhere else?

The easiest way to be anti-fragile is to diversify.

I used several social channels, including more than one video channel and a messaging channel. The point was not only to reach a different person on each one. Sometimes I wanted to reach the same person in a different place. If one connection went away, I did not want the whole relationship to go with it.

That is why a small channel can still matter. It may not produce the most views today. But it may give me another way to speak to people who already care about the work. I do not want a large following on one site to fool me into thinking I own the entire route to those people.

I took this idea into my own life as well. I liked the idea of being a citizen of the world rather than feeling trapped in one place. I spent time getting different arrangements in different countries and talked about having bank accounts in nineteen countries. I used multiple licences and passports as part of that story too.

I wanted options. Several licences, several accounts, different places I could go. But an option has to work when I need it. Another piece of paper does not make a restriction disappear. I need to understand the conditions of every route I rely on.

Back in the business, I used an equally large picture: eight companies, eight bank accounts, nine payment processors. Those numbers were a way to hammer home the dependence problem, not a calculation of the right setup for every small business. More accounts can also mean more work and more things to keep correct.

I called the idea being anti-fragile. For this part, the plain meaning is do not let one failure take every route down with it. Redundancy helps me continue; it does not automatically make every disruption profitable.

I want to ask the uncomfortable question while everything is working. If this service fails tomorrow, where do the orders go? Where does the message go? Who knows the next step? A backup that exists only in my imagination is another form of wishful thinking. A legitimate route that I understand gives me something I can actually use.

chapters.title: Lead the work. Keep the team sharp. Do something useful.
chapters.short: Effort, momentum, and the fish stall
chapters.intro: I want to set the standard myself. But the point of the work is a useful result, not an impressive headcount or a long performance of being busy.
chapters.takeaway: Show the standard, build capable people, and keep taking sensible next steps.
chapters.body:
It was around eleven at night while I was filming, and I had been working since seven in the morning, with gaps for errands. That is the picture behind my next point: if I am the person leading the thing, I cannot stand at the back and complain that nobody else is pushing.

The only way you can lead anything in life is from the front.

In the studio business, I saw the hours the performers did, but I also did the work around those hours. Technical problems, planning, ideas, presentation, and everything that needed organising. An owner can carry work that is less visible than the shift people see.

That still does not let me measure everyone else's effort by how tired I feel. If a company is slow, I want to see where the work actually goes. How much time disappears into repeated checking, unnecessary conversation, waiting, or unclear instructions? Adding another person is not always the answer to an inefficient method.

I get impatient with using discomfort as a reason never to finish. Done or not done. Finished or unfinished. That is the question I keep asking. When I was nineteen, I ran to work, ran home, ran to the gym, trained for three hours, then ran home again. I knew what putting effort into a day felt like.

But I am describing my drive, not proving that exhaustion is imaginary. If I turn every limit into an insult, I can lose the ability to tell whether the work is still good. The useful demand is to finish the important job; it is not to pretend people are machines.

There is also a difference in how winning feels. In a fight, when things were going well, I did not notice the tiredness in the same way. When I was taking a beating, everything felt harder. Business can feel similar. A busy order book gives the work feedback. A quiet room can make the same effort feel pointless.

You do not want an army. You want special forces.

That is why the slow beginning matters. It is easier to keep going when the orders are already flying in. I need a method for working through the period before that. A useful first result can help motivation more than another speech about having the right mindset.

Then I need the right size of team. At one point I had seventy-two performers and described a month with around 600,000 in turnover. It looked large. It was also expensive. There were rents, management layers, big percentages, and more people than I could give proper attention to.

I ended up keeping the top ten. I enjoyed the company more, and it became more profitable. I had less scale to point at, but less overhead and a group I could actually work with closely. A bigger number on the team sheet is not a better result by itself.

I like capable people who can do more than one thing. Train them well. Give them a clear job. Understand what they need to work properly. I would rather have a compact team that can act than a large team that needs endless coordination.

I learned the last part of this at my uncle's fish stall when I was fifteen. My job was moving boxes of ice. When I had finished, I stood around. He asked what I was doing. I said I had finished the work. He told me there was always something else: wipe the wall, sweep the floor, find the next useful task.

There's always work to do.

I brought that into my own teams. If one answer is missing, find an appropriate next action. Improve the copy. Follow up a real enquiry. Prepare something the team needs. I used sixty percent right against zero percent as a rough illustration: a sensible imperfect step can be better than standing still.

The word sensible matters. Sending rubbish everywhere is still rubbish. I want movement towards the job, with enough judgment to avoid creating a bigger mess. Edit something. Produce something useful. Let a practical step replace the long conversation about why nothing has happened.

chapters.title: Give people a reason to look. Give them a reason to trust.
chapters.intro: Curiosity can make an ordinary offer interesting. Trust asks a different question: can people rely on what I say, and can they rely on me when it matters?
chapters.takeaway: Create interest honestly, explain my real contribution, and make reliability mutual.
chapters.body:
I want some curiosity in the way I present an offer. If I call a course a collection of secrets, I am creating a question in the buyer's mind. What does this person know? What could I learn that I have not already seen? It sounds different from a dry list of contents.

Even a bouncy ball can open that kind of question. Come and see why this one is different. Now someone may want to look. But once they look, there needs to be an actual difference or an honestly presented experience. Curiosity gets attention; it cannot manufacture a better ball.

Curiosity sells.

I used the same idea with a book and a free special gift. People want to know what the extra is. In creator work, a preview can also give people a reason to see the full experience. I am pointing towards the gap between what they know and what they would like to discover.

People are nosy.

I still need to make the purchase clear. If the only thing I have is a mystery, the buyer cannot judge the offer. I want enough interest to make them look and enough information to let them decide. A useful promise beats a long fog of hints.

Then comes the question of credit. I have always pushed people not to throw away the value of their own achievements. If a customer tells me something worked well, I should not automatically shrug and make the work sound accidental. If I did the thinking and the execution, I can say so.

I used an extreme bouncy-ball example: the customer says it bounces two millimetres higher, and I act as though I expected it. That shows how easily a confident story can run ahead of what I actually knew. I can claim the work I did without pretending I controlled every lucky part of the outcome.

People will connect me with the bad result when something goes wrong. I want them to connect me with my real contribution when it goes right too. The aim is to make the value visible, not to give myself imaginary powers.

Now look at the people beside me. I prefer a dependable person to a brilliant person I cannot rely on. Talent is attractive. But if the business needs me away for an emergency, I need to know the promises will still be kept.

Loyalty's both ways.

If I have a thousand in the bank and owe a worker a thousand, I pay the worker and go without. I do my part. They do their part. That is a much stronger basis for trust than simply demanding that somebody be loyal to me.

I have used relationships outside work to explain the same thing. Good looks, charm, or skill do not make up for a relationship where I expect the agreement to be broken. In business, I want people whose word means something. I also want to reward the people who have shown they can be counted on over time.

Reliability does not require somebody to give up every choice they have. It means being straight about the commitment and following through. I want capable people, and I want them to know I will stand behind the things I owe them. The foundation has to hold from both sides.

chapters.title: The owner needs income. The bills still exist.
chapters.short: Owner pay, debt, reputation, and morale
chapters.intro: I do not want years of work to leave me with nothing outside a fragile company. But I also cannot confuse the account balance with money free of every obligation.
chapters.takeaway: Know what belongs to fulfilment, what is owed, and what can really support the owner.
chapters.body:
I go back to the first television agency here because it taught me a painful lesson. I was so occupied with keeping the thing afloat that money kept going back into it. When it finally failed, I had not built the personal cushion I thought years of running a business should have produced.

When that agency collapsed, I kept thinking about the money I could have kept. Nearly a million. I was angry with myself. But anger does not change the arithmetic: cash in the account can still be owed to staff, suppliers, and customers. I need to know what is actually free before I call it mine.

If the company blew up today, what would I be sitting on?

That is the question I want an owner to face. If the answer is nothing, look at the structure. Am I earning anything from the work? Am I reinvesting into something sound, or feeding a hole? Do I know what it costs to finish the promises already made?

I'm not saying don't reinvest in your company.

My frustration was with becoming so attached to the company that I forgot why I had built it. A company can become my baby. I can keep rescuing it because closing it feels like admitting something about myself. That does not make the next rescue a good use of money.

Now look at debt. I knew a trader. He imported ordinary goods, including wind-up torches, and found places to sell them. He would ignore invoices until the supplier threatened a court case. Sometimes that meant months of waiting. He protected the cash in his account by making somebody else carry the delay.

That is not free money. The other business still has wages and bills. I had been on that side of the relationship myself, waiting for large clients while my own staff needed paying. A ninety-day payment process feels very different when the money is owed to me.

I had apartments I no longer needed for the studio. I owed three months of rent, around 6,000 altogether. I told the landlord I could pay 2,000. He asked about 3,000. We eventually settled at 2,500.

I settled that bill at 2,500. That was an agreement with that landlord. It was not permission to wipe every debt off my books. If we have not agreed new terms, the bill is still there.

A temporary bank balance can look like wealth when I stop looking at the bills. Do not play that game with yourself. If I hide the obligations, I cannot tell whether the business works. I need the true cash position in front of me.

Reputation is tied into it too. I knew some people mattered to future trading relationships, and I thought about whether a dispute would travel. But a distant supplier is still a person on the other side of an agreement. Distance does not turn the relationship into nothing.

I do not want the company to be rich on paper while I am broke. I also do not want to call the owner rich because obligations have been pushed out of sight. Work out the true position. That tells me much more than staring at the biggest number in the account.

Finally, I come back to the mood of the team. In the little office, my positive energy mattered. When I walked in, spoke about the next deal, and made people feel the work was moving, the room changed. When I left, that energy vanished.

I can call that my people-management lesson: the leader's behaviour spreads. But a good mood cannot replace clear expectations or money I owe. Positivity can support a working team. It cannot carry the entire arrangement on its own. The ten-day absence had already shown me what happens when the arrangement is too thin underneath the enthusiasm.

chapters.title: Change the presentation. Match the person. Explain the need now.
chapters.short: The pen, the chessboard, and the final car example
chapters.intro: I finish this stretch by returning to the way an offer is presented. The same item can mean different things to different people, and a distant benefit may not answer the problem on their mind today.
chapters.takeaway: Use the right strengths, understand the buyer’s real goal, and make the present value concrete.
chapters.body:
People ask me what they should sell. I ask how they could sell. What reach do they have? What do people already come to them for? Which useful product could fit that route? The object matters, but the way it reaches the buyer and the meaning around it can matter too.

I pick up a pen as an example. I could talk about the plastic, the colour, and the ink. Or I could put a story around it: important contracts, ideas, and the work a person hopes to do with it. I used a price of $38. I was showing how an ordinary object can be given a very different place in the buyer's mind.

Play to people's strengths.

A story is not a magic feature. If I promise the pen will create million-dollar ideas, I have moved from explaining meaning to inventing a result. I do not need that claim to see the difference between a bare object and a relevant presentation.

In the studio, I had a performer who thought she had run out of things to sell. Videos had not worked. Other offers had not worked. I watched the questions people were asking and changed the setting and the story around the performance.

I moved her from the bedroom to the bathroom. She whispered, and we played out an invented risk of being interrupted. I even described knocking on the door as part of it. The audience reacted strongly, and she kept that setup for the next two months.

I didn't try and change the what, I changed the how.

I had been trying to find a new thing to sell. In the end, changing the way I presented the same thing was enough. I watched what people responded to, changed the setting, and kept the setup that worked.

Next I look at the people doing the work. A knight and a bishop do not move the same way on a chessboard. I win by understanding what each piece can do, rather than ordering both to behave identically. The same thought applies to a team.

Some people handle pressure well. Some are good at adapting. Some can explain. Some can make the thing look right. I am not particularly good with cameras and editing, so I hire creative people who can do those parts properly. Knowing what I want is not the same as knowing how to produce every frame.

I should know my own limits as clearly as I know my strengths. The job is to put the right ability on the right problem. Details matter, but relevant ability matters more than deciding what somebody should do from their appearance.

The buyer is different each time too. In the agency, if a company was already selling plenty, I might talk about profile, positioning, and what a campaign could mean in its category. If another company desperately wanted more sales, I would not give it the same long speech about prestige. I would talk about reaching customers and what we could realistically do for that goal.

I used a simple question: are you selling enough? Usually the answer was that they would like to sell more. Now I knew something about what they wanted. That was the opening. It did not prove television would solve every problem, but it told me which problem the buyer wanted to discuss.

The pen returns here as another reminder. A person staring at a blank page may care more about finding something worth writing than about how many months the ink lasts. I need to understand that desire, then be honest about how my offer relates to it. Confidence and curiosity can help someone look. They cannot create powers the product does not have.

Finally, I was discussing a back-end system with someone in one of my businesses. The conversation kept going towards what might happen in two years. I wanted to know what problem we were solving now. People have yesterday's trouble and tomorrow's bills on their minds. A distant possibility can feel very small beside those things.

Immediate, not later.

With television advertising, a prospect might say they were thinking about branding next year. I tried to bring the conversation back to a current reason to act. Timing can matter. But I need an actual reason, rather than simply making the buyer frightened that somebody else is ahead.

Future benefits can support the offer. I want the present benefit to be clear enough to lead it. What changes for the buyer now? What current cost, inconvenience, or goal does this address?

I never worked in car sales, although I thought I would be good at it. When I buy a car, I recognise the conversation. I say the car I have is fine and I might replace it next year. The salesperson points to what a change could mean now: fuel costs, tax, insurance, and the driving assistance on the new car. They are trying to turn a future purchase into a current decision by making today's value more concrete.
